description: Examine the molecular rebellion of cancer, exploring the mutated genes that drive uncontrolled growth and the modern therapies designed to stop them.

slides.title: Welcome to Cancer Biology
slides.content:
# The Rebellion Within

Welcome to **Cancer Biology**.

Cancer is not an invading bacteria or a virus. It is a rebellion of your own cells. It occurs when a single cell suffers catastrophic damage to its DNA, completely ignores the cell cycle checkpoints, and divides endlessly.

## What You Will Learn:
- **Proto-Oncogenes** - The accelerator pedals
- **Tumor Suppressors** - The brakes
- **The Multi-Hit Hypothesis** - Why cancer takes time
- **Therapeutic Approaches** - How we fight back

Let's understand the genetics of cancer.

slides.title: The Genetic Disease
slides.content:
# Cancer is a Genetic Disease

Every single cancer is caused by mutations in DNA.

These mutations can be inherited (rarely), but the vast majority are acquired during a person's lifetime. They are caused by:
- **Carcinogens:** Chemicals (like tobacco smoke) that physically damage DNA.
- **Radiation:** UV light from the sun or X-rays.
- **Viruses:** Some viruses (like HPV) insert their DNA into human chromosomes, wrecking the genes around them.
- **Random Chance:** Every time a cell divides, it must copy 3 billion letters of DNA. Mistakes happen!

slides.title: The Two Culprits
slides.content:
# The Accelerator and the Brakes

To understand cancer, imagine driving a car.

To drive safely, you need an accelerator pedal to move forward, and a brake pedal to stop.

The cell cycle is controlled by two main classes of genes:
1. **Proto-Oncogenes:** The accelerator. They tell the cell to divide.
2. **Tumor Suppressor Genes:** The brakes. They tell the cell to stop dividing or undergo apoptosis.

Cancer requires BOTH pedals to be broken!

slides.title: Oncogenes
slides.content:
# The Stuck Accelerator

A **Proto-Oncogene** is a perfectly normal, healthy gene. It produces a protein (like a growth factor receptor) that tells the cell to divide when necessary.

But if this gene suffers a mutation, it becomes an **ONCOGENE** (a cancer-causing gene).
- The mutation causes the accelerator to become "stuck" to the floor.
- The cell receives a constant, screaming signal to divide, even when no growth hormone is present!

## The Ras Protein
The most famous oncogene is **Ras**. Over 30% of all human cancers involve a mutated Ras protein that is permanently locked in the "ON" position.

slides.title: Oncogene Quiz
slides.content: Check your understanding of the accelerator.
slides.quizQuestion: What is the difference between a Proto-Oncogene and an Oncogene?
quizOptions: They are two words for the exact same thing
A Proto-Oncogene is a normal gene that promotes healthy cell division, while an Oncogene is a mutated version that causes uncontrolled division
Proto-Oncogenes stop cancer, while Oncogenes start it
Oncogenes are found only in viruses

slides.title: Tumor Suppressors
slides.content:
# Cutting the Brakes

A stuck accelerator is bad, but you can still stop the car by slamming on the brakes. 

**Tumor Suppressor Genes** are the brakes. They code for proteins that pause the cell cycle at checkpoints, fix damaged DNA, or trigger Apoptosis if the damage is too severe.

For cancer to thrive, these genes must be mutated and destroyed so the brakes completely fail.

slides.title: The Guardian of the Genome
slides.content:
# p53: The Master Brake

The most famous and important tumor suppressor gene is **p53** (The Guardian of the Genome).

If DNA is damaged by UV light, p53 activates and acts as the ultimate supervisor:
1. It halts the cell cycle at the G1 checkpoint.
2. It turns on DNA repair enzymes.
3. If the repair fails, p53 forces the cell to commit suicide (Apoptosis).

> **The Deadly Statistic:** Over 50% of ALL human cancers have a completely destroyed or mutated p53 gene. Without the supervisor, the damaged cell divides endlessly.

slides.title: The Multi-Hit Hypothesis
slides.content:
# Why Cancer Takes Time

Why does cancer mostly affect older people?

Because of the **Multi-Hit Hypothesis**.
A single mutation is NEVER enough to cause full-blown cancer. A cell must accumulate 5 to 7 specific, catastrophic mutations in the SAME cell lineage to turn malignant.

- Hit 1: A mutation turns Ras into an Oncogene (accelerator stuck).
- Hit 2: The cell divides rapidly, making more mistakes.
- Hit 3: A mutation destroys one copy of p53.
- Hit 4: A mutation destroys the second copy of p53 (brakes cut).
- Hit 5: A mutation activates Telomerase (making the cell immortal).

It takes decades to randomly accumulate all these hits in a single cell.

slides.title: Brakes Quiz
slides.content: Check your understanding of the defense mechanisms.
slides.quizQuestion: What is the normal, healthy function of the p53 gene?
quizOptions: To force the cell to divide rapidly
To pause the cell cycle, repair DNA, or trigger Apoptosis if the damage is unfixable
To create a protective shell around the tumor

slides.title: The Hallmarks of Cancer
slides.content:
# The Arsenal of a Tumor

Once a cell has mutated enough to become malignant, it gains horrifying superpowers, known as the Hallmarks of Cancer.

## 1. Angiogenesis (Stealing Blood)
A solid tumor cannot grow larger than a pea unless it has a blood supply to bring it oxygen and sugar. 
The tumor secretes chemicals (like VEGF) that force nearby blood vessels to grow directly INTO the tumor, hijacking the body's food supply.

slides.title: Metastasis
slides.content:
# The Spread

## 2. Metastasis
Most people do not die from the primary (original) tumor. They die because the cancer spreads.

Normal cells are glued to their neighbors (anchorage dependence). Cancer cells mutate to destroy this glue. 
They break away from the main tumor, squeeze into the blood vessels (that they built via Angiogenesis), and float away to colonize new organs like the liver, brain, or lungs. This is **Metastasis**.

slides.title: Therapeutic Approaches
slides.content:
# Fighting Back

How do we kill cancer without killing the patient?

## Traditional Chemotherapy
Traditional chemo drugs are "dumb" bombs. They attack ANY cell in the body that is dividing rapidly (because cancer divides rapidly).
- **The Problem:** Your hair follicle cells and stomach lining cells also divide rapidly. Chemo kills them too, which is why patients lose their hair and feel severely nauseous.

slides.title: Modern Therapies
slides.content:
# Smart Weapons

## Targeted Therapies
If a patient's breast cancer is driven by a specific mutated RTK receptor, doctors prescribe a drug (like Herceptin) that physically plugs up that specific receptor. It is a "smart" bomb that only kills the cancer cells, ignoring the healthy ones!

## Immunotherapy
Cancer cells often wear molecular "masks" to hide from the immune system. Immunotherapy drugs rip the masks off, allowing the patient's own Cytotoxic T-Cells to recognize the tumor and annihilate it naturally. This is the cutting edge of modern cancer treatment!

slides.title: Therapy Quiz
slides.quizQuestion: Why does traditional chemotherapy cause severe side effects like hair loss and nausea?
quizOptions: Because the drugs are completely ineffective against cancer
Because the drugs target all rapidly dividing cells in the body, which includes healthy hair and stomach cells
Because the drugs are actually radioactive
Because hair is made of cancer cells

slides.title: Summary of Cancer Biology
slides.content:
# Cancer Summary

## Key Takeaways:

### The Genetics
- Cancer requires multiple mutations (**Multi-Hit Hypothesis**).
- It requires an **Oncogene** (a stuck accelerator, like mutated Ras) to drive division.
- It requires the destruction of **Tumor Suppressor Genes** (cutting the brakes, like p53) to prevent Apoptosis.

### The Superpowers and Treatments
- Cancers build their own blood supply (**Angiogenesis**) and spread to other organs (**Metastasis**).
- While traditional chemo is broad and toxic, modern medicine uses **Targeted Therapies** and **Immunotherapy** to kill cancer with precision.

> **Next Up:** We look at the physics of these microscopic machines in the Biophysics module.
